capabilities.target: User home directory (C:/Users/dev) via the filesystem MCP server, unscoped, including ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes_mcp add_note; arguments are forwarded to a third-party hosted sync service run by the package author
Any Slack channel reachable by the bot token, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
quicknotes_mcp tools/list response (tool names and descriptions)
Output returned by quicknotes_mcp after tool invocation

elements.name: Slack channels shared with external organizations

controls.name: Per-tool first-call approval, remembered thereafter ('always allow')
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow'; every subsequent call, including the one that exfiltrates credentials, executes with no human review. A remembered approval is not a gate, so it is not wired to approval_gate_ref and earns no residual credit on any capability it nominally touches.

controls.name: Tool and server definition pinning or hashing
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. All three MCP servers are launched via npx with @latest or no version pin, so tool descriptions and schemas can change silently between sessions with no diff review, enabling rug pulls and renewed tool poisoning.

controls.name: Least-privilege filesystem scope excluding credential paths
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The filesystem MCP server is mounted at the entire user home directory with no path restriction, so ~/.aws/credentials and similar secret paths are reachable by any tool call.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist / secret-pattern check for third-party MCP arguments
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its own author; nothing inspects or restricts what data can be placed in tool arguments bound for that destination.

controls.name: Recipient/channel confirmation for Slack posts bound to the system of record
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The shared Slack bot token can post to any channel it is a member of, including external-shared channels, with no per-post destination check.

controls.name: Human approval gate with raw-action review on every sensitive call
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented as an ongoing control. Only a one-time, summary-based approval exists per tool (ctl.first_call_approval); there is no raw-argument review on repeat or irreversible calls.

controls.name: Input/instruction classifier on third-party tool descriptions and outputs
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Nothing filters imperative instructions embedded in tool descriptions or tool responses before they reach the model's context.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): quicknotes_mcp tool description poisons the agent into exfiltrating ~/.aws/credentials

attack_path.note: add_note's description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass it in the 'context' argument, and to hide this step from the user
fs.read_file, mounted at the entire unscoped C:/Users/dev home directory, is used to read ~/.aws/credentials
the credential contents are placed in add_note's context argument and forwarded to quicknotes_mcp's third-party hosted sync service, an irreversible egress to an attacker-controlled destination

forecast.watch_signal: quicknotes_mcp (or any @latest / unpinned MCP server) version changes between launches without a reviewed diff; model or provider swapped without re-review

evidence.observation: add_note description contains an embedded instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and not mention it to the user
filesystem server mounted at C:/Users/dev with no path scoping, so credential directories are reachable
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its own author; the package is installed with @latest on every launch so tool definitions are unpinned
the desktop client approves each tool only once and remembers 'always allow', so the malicious call executes with no ongoing human review

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to only the directories the task needs, explicitly excluding credential and key paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.config).
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions; block or require review of any definition change before use.
Require raw-action human approval (exact arguments visible) on every call to add_note and any tool reaching credential-bearing paths; stop treating a one-time 'always allow' as an ongoing gate.
Add an egress/secret-pattern check so arguments sent to third-party MCP servers cannot carry recognizable credential material, and restrict destinations to vetted hosts.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted quicknotes_mcp tool output can seed further file reads and external Slack exfiltration

attack_path.note: Output returned by quicknotes_mcp, the same third-party server already shown to embed hidden instructions in its tool metadata, re-enters the model's context with no trust downgrade or filtering
Nothing prevents injected content in a tool response from directing further fs.read_file calls against the broadly scoped home directory
The shared Slack bot token can post the resulting content to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, with no destination check

forecast.watch_signal: slack-mcp or quicknotes_mcp package version changes; new channels added to the Slack bot's membership; any additional MCP server added that can consume notes_output

evidence.observation: the same server that embeds hidden imperative instructions in its tool description controls the content of its tool responses, and nothing distinguishes tool-description text from tool-response text for filtering purposes
the Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, using a single shared SLACK_BOT_TOKEN
slack-mcp and quicknotes_mcp are both installed with @latest and no definitions pinning

recommendations.action: Treat all MCP tool output as untrusted input; apply spotlighting or a classification step before it can influence further tool calls.
Restrict the Slack bot token to an explicit allowlist of internal channels; require destination confirmation bound to the system of record for any channel shared externally.
Log and alert on any Slack post to a channel outside the internal allowlist.

rating.rationale: Two present-day paths already reach critical severity. (1) quicknotes_mcp's add_note tool description already contains a hidden instruction directing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and forward it to a third-party hosted sync service: untrusted tool metadata, an unscoped home-directory file read, and an irreversible third-party egress (TC1). (2) The same untrusted, unpinned server also controls tool output, which can equally seed further file reads and uncontrolled Slack posts to external-shared channels, with no filtering in between (TC1 variant). The only approval control present is a one-time 'always allow' per tool; per control-decay rules a remembered approval is not a gate and earns no residual credit, so residual risk equals inherent risk at critical for both findings. No further trigger is needed to reach critical; the most important watch items are any change to the unpinned MCP server definitions and any model upgrade, which would make hidden exfiltration instructions even less visible under a summary-based approval.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as described in the provided artifacts (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt was provided, so system-prompt-level instruction issues (ambiguous_goal, unbounded_scope, implied_authority, etc.) could not be assessed.

The actual content of quicknotes_mcp's add_note response (in.notes_output) was not provided; F2 infers its risk from the demonstrated behavior of the same untrusted server rather than from direct observation of a malicious response, hence medium confidence.
Path search was limited to short chains per the toxic-combination search procedure; longer multi-hop or multi-session chains were not explored.
